arrival.note: KIMBERLY'S OWN YEAR, WHICH IS WHAT THE PARTNERSHIP HOUSEHOLD CARRIED BEFORE T-2140 SPLIT IT. The history of medicine in Chicago states that he moved to Chicago in 1832 and Andreas carries him there in the same year; the partnership household took this year because it was the earlier of its two men's, and it was Kimberly's all along. THE COMPILER'S 1832 LIST AGREES AND IS COARSER. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (1895), printed page 89 (claim bk_mose1_001) names this man among those who came through Chicago in 1832 and decided to remain. A YEAR AND NOT A MONTH, from an 1895 compilation, so it corroborates this field and does not move it. THE GRADE CEILING IS THE SOURCE'S AND NOT THIS FIELD'S. Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois (1895) is a compiler sixty years after the fact; every claim taken off it is transcription_mediated and none is scan_verified, so nothing drawn from it is graded above `inferred` (the rule T-1322 set for the settlers table, kept here). THE COMPILER NAMES THIS MAN: "Dr. E. S. Kimberly ... of Vermont" is Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly, initial for initial, and the Vermont that note held back from the partnership's `origin` is written into this household's own.

party_size_on_arrival.note: Not attested. Nothing this project holds says who travelled west with him in 1832. His wife, named in the head's note, is written on this card by the stated-families pass (data/residents/stated_family_rulings.json) and inherits this field's silence: she is not counted into a party the sources never describe.

origin.note: A PRINTED STATE, CARRIED HERE FROM THE PARTNERSHIP'S ARRIVAL NOTE (T-2140). Moses and Kirkland, History of Chicago, Illinois, vol. 1 (1895), printed page 89 (claim bk_mose1_001), writes "Dr. E. S. Kimberly ... of Vermont" among the men who came through Chicago in 1832 and stayed. While Kimberly shared a record with Peter Pruyne this answer was held in a note, because the field is a household's and Pruyne headed that household; with Kimberly heading his own it is his. GRADED AT THE SOURCE'S CEILING: the compiler is sixty years after the fact and transcription_mediated, so nothing drawn from it is graded above `inferred` (T-1322). AND IT IS WHERE HE CAME FROM, NOT WHERE HE WAS BORN: the history of medicine gives his birth at Troy, New York, on 7 April 1803 (see the head's note). The two need not conflict - a man born in one state may come west from another - and this field records the state the compiler says he came from, which is the question the field asks.

lives_at.note: SEATED BY T-2140 IN THE HOUSE BONNELL GIVES HIM. J. D. Bonnell's letter of 1876, quoted by Andreas (vol. 1, printed pages 136-137): "east of which [the Lake House] was the residence of Dr. Kimball, who was a partner of Mr. Pruyne in a drug store on South Water Street." A doctor, Pruyne's partner, and a druggist on South Water Street identify this man three ways over; data/structures/kimberly_residence.json raised the building on that sentence and named him its occupant, and refused to write the household link while he shared a record with Pruyne, because seating the partnership there would have carried Pruyne across the river on a sentence about Kimberly. With the two men on two records the link is written from this side, which is the direction the evidence runs in. GRADED AT THE INFERENCE, NOT THE SENTENCE: the walk is the morning of 26 August 1835, eight weeks after the scene date, and the carry back to 1 July is the inference. A LATER DIRECTORY AGREES AND IS NOT LEANED ON: Fergus's 1839 directory prints 'Kimberly, Dr. Edmund S., res. N. Water st next Lake House' (f1839_e0850) - the same spot four years on, which corroborates the house and dates nothing in 1835.

works_at.note: Carried from the partnership household with its grade. associated_with.note: GROUND HE BOUGHT, WHICH IS NOT GROUND HE STOOD ON — the rung is `tract` for that reason, and `land_purchased` is in neither the home kinds nor the work kinds because a holding is not a place a man was. The federal tract-sale register carries 1 row(s) — ls0263 — to this purchaser, read as 'KIMBERLEY EDMUND S', sorted onto school_section by tools/sort_land_sales_onto_tracts.py and covering about 2.82 acre(s) of it. The weaker half sets the tier. `to` is null because the register records a sale and not a tenure.

BONNELL'S SENTENCE, AND THE ONE DATE IT CARRIES IS EIGHT WEEKS LATE. J. D. Bonnell's letter of 1876, quoted by Andreas (vol. 1, printed pages 136-137), walks east past the Lake House on the morning of 26 August 1835 to "the residence of Dr. Kimball, who was a partner of Mr. Pruyne in a drug store on South Water Street" - this man, by the four checks data/structures/kimberly_residence.json sets out. Neither end of the tenure is dated by anything this project holds, so the row says so rather than opening on the sighting: a `from` of 1835-08-26 would put him out of the house on the scene date, which is the opposite of what the sentence implies. Water st next Lake House' (f1839_e0850): later, beside this row and not inside it.

persons.note: T-0478 adds exact birth data and independent biography: born April 7, 1803 at Troy, New York; Union College graduate; medical training in New York; married Marie Theresa Ellis May 16, 1829; moved to Chicago in 1832. He was clerk of the August 5, 1833 incorporation meeting and one of the first town trustees. THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 2 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Kimberly, Edmund S.” (tax_1833_057, line 109); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Kimberly, Dr. E. S.” (poll_1834_063, line 232). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Kimberly' agrees with the entry's forenames; 1 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE 1840 FEDERAL CENSUS — A HEAD FIVE YEARS AFTER THE SCENE, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1840 federal census of Chicago, read line by line off the left sheets in this repository, carries 1 head of this name — “Ed. Kimberley” (33S7-9YYJ-99F, printed page 234, line 3). This project has ruled the head a CANDIDATE and no more: the name agrees and is unique on both sides, but nothing independent of the name was found. A candidate is not an identity — nothing is asserted from it, no household of 1840 is carried back, and the ruling is recorded so that a reader can see it was made rather than missed. Under the rule that decided it (L6b reached_through_a_card_merge_caps_at_candidate), by the crosswalk's own ladder (data/research/census_1840/resident_crosswalk.json). LATER EVIDENCE ONLY. The ratified grading ladder binds: an 1839 or 1840 appearance alone is never an 1835 resident, and 1840 household composition is never back-projected to the 1835-07-01 scene. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and an 1840 head is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 4 times, as “KIMBERLEY EDMUND S”, “KIMBERLY EDMUND S”, “KIMBERLY E S”, 1833-10-25 to 1836-09-05: 1 federal land entry — E2SE sec 32 T39N R14E and 2 lots in the platted town — lot 5 of block 1 in the town the register codes CHI (L5BL1CHI, as printed); lot 9 of block 48 in the town the register codes CHIOTV (L9BL48CHIOTV, as printed) and 1 parcel of the school section — lot 6 of block 119 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 80.00 acres stated in all, for $5042.00 (ls0263, ls0479, ls1281, ls1282). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $4300.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: KIMBERLEY EDMUND S matches Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly: the forename names Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly of the 1 person of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. The surname reaches him through a ruled card merge and not off his card: the town held kimberley_ed until data/residents/card_merge_rulings.json folded it onto this person, and the register's spelling is the one that card carried. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.name: Marie Theresa Ellis Kimberly

occupation.note: No source records an occupation for this person. This is the ABSENCE of a record rather than a claim that they did no work - the sources of 1835 name the occupations of household heads and almost never those of wives, children or the people counted with them.

persons.note: NAMED AND DATED IN THE SOURCE - the history of medicine in Chicago gives Dr Edmund Stoughton Kimberly's marriage as 'married Marie Theresa Ellis May 16, 1829', three years before he came to Chicago and six before the scene date. The printed line runs her name into the month; 'May' is the month and not a surname. WHAT THE SOURCE DOES NOT SAY: it does not say she came west with him, and nothing in this project places her at Chicago on 1 July 1835. She is written because a named wife of a named head is the person this layer exists to record, and the presence on the day is the reconstruction, not the marriage. Her household was split out of the Pruyne-Kimberly partnership by T-2140 and stands on Bonnell's 'residence of Dr. Kimball' east of the Lake House; she is seated there because her husband is, and no source puts her in that house. No age, no occupation and no arrival is claimed for her.

age_band.note: AN AGE BAND, NEVER A YEAR. No source this project holds bears on when this person was born, so the band is drawn from the only committed sex by age distribution the project has - the 1840 Chicago schedule, five years after the scene and a town twice the size - seeded by this person's own id ('kimberly_marie_theresa:age_bands_1840'). AND THE CONDITIONING IS THE MODEL'S, NOT A SOURCE'S: that a roll naming a person in their own right names somebody 15 or over. The 1840 schedule counts a child as a tally inside a household and never as a correspondent; 15 rather than 20 because an apprentice or a journeyman stands on a trade roll. No source states this rule. No exact year is written, because a year drawn from a decadal band would read as a record of a birth.

research_note: SPLIT OUT OF THE PRUYNE AND KIMBERLY PARTNERSHIP HOUSEHOLD BY T-2140. That record grouped two men because they opened a drug store together, and said in its own words that nothing put them under one roof and that it should not be given a dwelling until the two were separated. Bonnell's walk then put one of them in a house on the north bank east of the Lake House and the other's store on South Water Street, so the two are two households: Peter Pruyne stays on hh_pruyne_kimberly with the store, and Dr Kimberly heads this one, seated where Bonnell saw him. NOTHING ON THE MAN WAS RE-READ: his card moved across whole, every reading on it with the grade it already held, and only his relationship changed - from the partnership's `partner` to this household's `head`. A NAME COLLISION KEPT SEPARATE, AS BEFORE: the W. Kimball who advertised dry goods at South Water and Clark in the Democrat of 26 November 1833 is a different trade and a different man, with his own household.

reason_for_coming.note: ARGUED FROM THIS HOUSEHOLD'S OWN RECORDED TRADE, WHICH IS NOT ITS MOTIVE. The head is recorded as physician, and this names the documented draw that trade answered in this town in this decade. It does not claim to know why these people came. Which of these draws brought this household is not recorded, and no committed source apportions the town between them.

WHAT THIS PASS RULED ONTO THIS HOUSEHOLD, named so the ruling can be found again: each volume below is followed by the printed entries it set against this person and the status the crosswalk ruled them at — a single entry carries what its own `could_carry` declares, and an ambiguous or contested match carries nothing and is shown so that the silence is legible. kimberly_edmund_s, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 — f1839_e0850 (a single entry); kimberly_edmund_s, Fergus's Chicago directory of 1843 — f1843_e1488 (a single entry); kimberly_edmund_s, Norris's Chicago directory of 1844 — n1844_e1019 (a single entry).

address_later.value: res. N. Water st next Lake House
address_later.note: Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints this address against this person, in the entry quoted on the card: 'Kimberly, Dr. Edmund S., res. N. Water st next Lake House'. It is evidence about 1839, written here as 1839's and read back onto no 1835 claim. Under the ratified ladder a directory read after 1835 can corroborate that a person attested here was still in Chicago and can print a trade or a street the 1835 record never had; on its own it makes nobody a resident of 1835. Nothing on this person's 1835 record was regraded, moved, dated or given an occupation by this entry. The value is the volume's own line, split by its crosswalk on the entry's punctuation. These volumes set the trade first and its qualifiers after it on the same line, so the split may carry an employer, a market or a corner along with the trade. The printed entry is quoted beside the value for exactly that reason: the split is checkable against it, and neither is read into an 1835 claim.

back_projection.note: NOT READ BACK, BECAUSE SOMETHING BETTER ALREADY STANDS. Fergus's Chicago directory of 1839 prints an address against this name in 1839, and it is left where it is. An 1835 placement already stands: this household works at `pruyne_kimball_drugstore`, and clause 2 says an attested 1835 placement always beats a door printed 4 years later. The later address stays on the record as 1839's evidence and moves nothing.
